title: December Lifts Your Revenue. It Quietly Lifts Your Stock Losses Too.
excerpt: A busier trading month always lifts the top line. It also quietly lifts breakage, miscounts and stock loss, a margin leak most owner-led businesses only discover weeks later, at the next count.
content:
Black Friday has come and gone, the shopfronts and online carts along the east coast are filling up for Christmas, and revenue for the next five weeks is about to look very healthy. It usually does. More customers move through the business, more stock moves off the shelf or out of the warehouse, and more transactions clear through the till than in any other month of the year.

What rarely gets talked about in the same breath is that the same volume lifting revenue is also lifting something else: the rate at which stock quietly goes missing. Breakage, miscounts, items picked incorrectly, product that never makes it from the back of house to the sale, the pattern we see across busy trading periods is that stock loss tracks volume, not any single person's actions. It is a feature of handling more, not a sign anyone did anything wrong.

The problem is not that this happens. It is that almost nobody is watching it happen in real time, which means a genuinely strong December can be quietly funding a margin leak that nobody notices until long after the decorations come down.

Where the Extra Movement Actually Goes

A business handling triple its usual stock volume in December is not just moving three times the product. It is creating three times the opportunities for a box to be miscounted on arrival, a fragile item to be damaged in the rush, a return to be put back on the shelf without being checked, or a pick to go out against the wrong line. More of the floor is often covered by casual or seasonal staff who have not yet built the same instinct for where stock quietly leaks as the regular team has, through no fault of their own. None of these individually move the needle. Multiplied across thousands of extra transactions in a five week window, they add up to a number that is bigger than it looks from any single incident.

Why It Doesn't Show Up Until the Next Count

Stock loss is one of the few costs in a business that does not announce itself. It does not appear as a line item on an invoice or a wage run. It sits quietly inside cost of goods sold until the next physical count reconciles what should be on the shelf against what actually is, and only then does the gap become a number. Your bookkeeper or BAS agent will record that variance accurately once it is counted, which is exactly the job that function is there to do. Spotting the drift while it is still happening, between counts, in the middle of the busiest trading window of the year, is a different job entirely, and it is one that usually goes unassigned. The monthly P&L keeps looking fine right up until the count that proves it was not.

What a Small Percentage Actually Costs

Take a business doing 500,000 dollars in revenue across the Christmas trading period, carrying stock loss that quietly rises from around 1 percent of sales in a normal month to 2 percent during the volume surge. That is the difference between a 5,000 dollar leak and a 10,000 dollar one, an extra 5,000 dollars gone before a single discount or wage cost is even considered. On a business running an 8 to 10 percent net margin, that single extra percentage point of stock loss is a material share of the month's actual profit, not a rounding error buried in the cost of goods sold line. A service business carrying materials or consumables instead of retail stock faces the same mechanics on a smaller scale, through wasted product, over-ordered supplies, or jobs that quietly use more than was quoted.

Checking the Leak Before Stocktake Finds It For You

The businesses that keep this leak small tend to do one thing differently: they check stock levels against sales at least once during the peak, not just at the scheduled count afterwards. A spot count on the highest-volume lines, a quick reconciliation of what was received against what was sold, catches a drift early enough to still do something about it. A Profit Pulse Check is built for exactly this kind of question, a focused look at where margin is actually leaking across the last twelve months, ranked by dollar impact, rather than a general sense that things feel tighter than the revenue suggests.

None of this is a reason to be nervous about a strong trading month. It is a reason to make sure the strength shows up in the margin, not just the revenue line. Checking that the two are moving together, during the peak rather than three months after it, is the kind of recurring discipline a fractional CFO brings to a business in the lead up to its busiest weeks of the year.

faqs.q: What counts as shrinkage or stock loss in a small Australian business?
faqs.a: Shrinkage is any stock that disappears between being received and being sold without a matching sale or recorded reason: breakage, miscounts, incorrect picks, items returned to shelf without checking, or product that simply cannot be accounted for. It sits inside cost of goods sold and rarely gets its own line, which is exactly why it tends to go unnoticed until a stock count forces the question.

faqs.q: Is a higher rate of stock loss normal during busy trading periods like Christmas?
faqs.a: There is no fixed normal figure, and treating one as a benchmark can be misleading. What matters more is the trend inside your own business: comparing the rate of loss during a high-volume month against your quieter months tells you whether the increase is proportional to the extra handling, or whether something else is driving it. That comparison is the useful number, not an industry average.

faqs.q: Can a service business without physical stock still have a shrinkage problem?
faqs.a: Yes, though it looks different. Consumables, materials, equipment and work in progress can all leak value the same way physical stock does, through miscounts, waste, or jobs that quietly absorb more material than was quoted. A Profit Pulse Check looks at this kind of leakage across any cost line, not only in businesses holding retail inventory.

faqs.q: How often should a business count stock to catch a loss early?
faqs.a: For most owner-led businesses, one spot count on the highest-volume or highest-value lines during a peak trading period is enough to catch a meaningful drift before it compounds. Waiting for the next scheduled stocktake means any loss during the peak has already happened by the time it is counted, with no chance to act on it while it still mattered.

faqs.q: Why doesn't stock loss show up on the profit and loss statement straight away?
faqs.a: Stock loss is absorbed into cost of goods sold rather than recorded as its own expense, so it only becomes visible once a physical count reconciles what should be on hand against what actually is. Until that count happens, a business can be trading at a lower real margin than its monthly reporting suggests without any single number flagging it.

faqs.q: How can a fractional CFO help with margin leaks like stock loss?
faqs.a: A fractional CFO brings the habit of checking margin against revenue through the year, not only at the annual stocktake, so a leak like rising stock loss gets caught while there is still time to respond. That recurring oversight is particularly valuable through a business's highest-volume trading weeks, when small percentage shifts carry the largest dollar impact.
